claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
The initial alloy exhibits a favorable strength–ductility combination.
Boron or carbon additions can act as grain-boundary-pinning elements in the alloy.
Adding boron or carbon will produce grain-boundary pinning.
Adding boron or carbon will cause solute segregation at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary-pinning additions will reduce grain growth during thermal exposure.
Grain-boundary-pinning additions will prevent the formation of brittle phases or precipitates during thermal exposure.
Suppressing grain growth and brittle-phase or precipitate formation will maintain toughness under subsequent loading.
Suppressing grain growth and brittle-phase or precipitate formation will maintain resistance to cracking under subsequent loading.
After identical thermal exposure and loading, the modified alloy will have greater toughness than the alloy without the additions.
After identical thermal exposure and loading, the modified alloy will have greater resistance to cracking than the alloy without the additions.
The hypothesis applies to exposure at approximately 500–700 °C for approximately 100 hours, followed by tensile or impact loading.
The amount and identity of the pinning addition and its interactions with other elements or impurities may affect the outcome.
